498.title: God so loved (John 3:16–21)
498.hook: God so loved the world as to give his only begotten son
498.howItsDone: Catholics hear John 3:16 at Mass on the Solemnity of the Most Holy Trinity in one year of the cycle and on the Fourth Sunday of Lent in another, and the Catechism quotes it in explaining why the Word became flesh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anothen, born again and from above, and a teaching about wind and Spirit. Your line was the wind bloweth where it will. What did you notice you couldn't control? Day four hundred ninety-eight, and a new week.

John 3:16. On a cardboard sign behind the end zone. Printed on the bottom of a fast food cup. Painted under an athlete's eyes. Scribbled on a highway overpass. It turns up everywhere, and it gets cut down, over and over, to a chapter and a number. Today we take it back off the poster and read it where it actually sits: in the middle of a long night conversation, with a teacher named Nicodemus, who came by night, still in the room.
screen: `A SIGN BEHIND THE END ZONE.` → `REDUCED TO A NUMBER.` → `BACK INTO THE NIGHT TALK.`

segments.voice: Here it is in the Douay-Rheims: "For God so loved the world, as to give his only begotten Son; that whosoever believeth in him, may not perish, but may have life everlasting." Start with so. In English we hear so as so much, God loved the world so very much. Some readers point out that the Greek word can also mean in this way, like this. God loved the world like this: by giving. The love is measured by what it gave. Then the world. In John's Gospel, the world is the world that, as we read in the prologue, knew him not. God loves that world. Not a better world. This one. Then gave, and only begotten. Some readers hear an echo here of Abraham, asked to offer Isaac, his only son, whom he loved. The next line is just as important, and it almost never makes the posters: "For God sent not his Son into the world, to judge the world, but that the world may be saved by him." Not to judge. To save. John then speaks of light and darkness: people sometimes prefer the dark, because they don't want their deeds seen, and the one who does truth comes to the light. Here's something honest to know. John doesn't mark where Jesus's words to Nicodemus end and his own reflection begins, and readers still discuss it. Some Bibles print verse 16 in red, as Jesus speaking; others don't. Either way, the Church reads it at Mass, and the Catechism says the Word became flesh so that we might know God's love, and quotes this line.
screen: `SO: NOT ONLY HOW MUCH, BUT HOW.` · `THE WORLD THAT DIDN'T KNOW HIM.` · `NOT TO JUDGE, BUT TO SAVE.` · `WHERE DO HIS WORDS END?` · then, large: `GOD SO LOVED THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say for god so loved me. Settle, and breathe. Read the verse slowly in your mind: for God so loved the world. Then let the world get smaller. Your country. Your town. Your street. Your house. You. Some Christians pray it this way, putting their own name where the world is. If you pray, you can say it so: for God so loved me. If you don't, just notice what it's like to hear a sentence about love with you inside it. The bell holds the time.
Houtos. The Greek word for so in John 3:16: not only how much God loved, but how, by giving his only begotten Son. Today's word.
Your line: so loved the world. Today, when the news makes the world look unlovable, remember that the verse is about this world, not a better one. Day four hundred ninety-eight.

499.title: He must increase (John 3:22–30)
499.hook: John the Baptist rejoices to become less
499.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist on June 24 and Christmas on December 25, and preachers since Augustine have linked the two dates to John's words, he must increase, but I must decrease.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John 3:16 off the poster: houtos, God loved the world, this world, by giving. Your line was so loved the world. Did a hard headline get that answer? Day four hundred ninety-nine.

Someone starts something. A band, a small business, a ministry at church, a club at school. It grows because of them. Then someone new shows up, and people start following the newcomer instead. Friends come by, upset on the founder's behalf: did you see? Everyone's going over there now. Today John the Baptist's disciples bring him exactly that news, about the man he pointed out at the Jordan, and his answer turns their worry inside out.
screen: `SOMEONE STARTS SOMETHING.` → `A NEWCOMER DRAWS THE CROWD.` → `EVERYONE IS GOING OVER THERE.`

segments.voice: Jesus and his disciples are baptizing in Judea, and John is still baptizing nearby. John's disciples come to him: Rabbi, the one who was with you across the Jordan, the one you pointed out, he's baptizing, and all men come to him. There's worry in it. John answers first with a principle, in the Douay-Rheims: "A man cannot receive any thing, unless it be given him from heaven." Whatever we have is given. Then a picture from a wedding. The bride belongs to the bridegroom. The bridegroom's friend, the best man, doesn't sulk because the bride isn't his. He stands near, he hears the bridegroom's voice, and he's glad. This, John says, is my joy, and it is full. And then the line: "He must increase, but I must decrease." Must. It isn't a resigned sigh. In John's mouth it sounds like a plan, even a delight. Saint Augustine noticed something about the calendar. The Church celebrates John's birth on June twenty-fourth, just after the longest day of the year, when the daylight starts to shrink. It celebrates Jesus's birth in late December, just after the shortest day, when the light begins to grow. Augustine said the calendar itself preaches this verse: John's days decrease, Christ's increase. Where the dates came from is debated; Augustine simply read the fit as a sermon. On an ordinary day, the line has a use. Not every good thing has to have your name on it. Sometimes the right thing to do for something you love is to step aside and be glad.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give someone else the credit. Settle, and breathe. Think of a recent win you were part of. A project, a family dinner, a team result. Now find the person whose part got less notice than yours. Picture what they did. Let yourself be glad about it, the way the bridegroom's friend is glad, not grudging. Plan exactly how you'll name it: a message, a sentence in a meeting, a word at the table. If you pray, you can thank God for them. The bell holds the time.
Bridegroom's friend. John the Baptist's name for himself, the best man glad to stand near while the crowds went to the groom. Today's word.
Your line: my joy is full. Today, give someone else the credit out loud, and see if you can be glad about it. Day four hundred ninety-nine.

500.title: Living water (John 4:7–15)
500.hook: whoever drinks the water I give shall not thirst for ever
500.howItsDone: Catholics hear the woman at the well on the Third Sunday of Lent in Year A, often with adults preparing for baptism at Easter, and the Catechism turns to this scene early in its teaching on prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bridegroom's friend: he must increase, but I must decrease. Your line was my joy is full. Who got the credit from you? Day five hundred. Five hundred days on the path.

Noon in Samaria. About the sixth hour, John says. Jesus is tired from the road and sits down by Jacob's well, while his disciples go into the town to buy food. A woman of Samaria comes out with her jar to draw water. John adds a note that explains the distance between them: the Jews do not communicate with the Samaritans. A Jewish man, a Samaritan woman, and a well between them. And then he speaks to her, and his first words are a request.
screen: `NOON AT JACOB'S WELL.` → `A WOMAN COMES TO DRAW WATER.` → `A TIRED STRANGER SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: He says: "Give me to drink." In John's telling, the one with the gift begins by asking. She's startled. How do you, a Jew, ask a drink of me, a Samaritan woman? And he answers, in the Douay-Rheims: "If thou didst know the gift of God, and who he is that saith to thee, Give me to drink; thou perhaps wouldst have asked of him, and he would have given thee living water." Living water. Living water can mean plain running water: a spring, a stream, water that moves, not still water in a cistern. She takes him that way, literally and very practically. Sir, you have nothing to draw with, and the well is deep. Are you greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well? He doesn't argue about Jacob. He points at the bucket. Whoever drinks this water will be thirsty again. Tomorrow at noon she'll be back with the jar. But, he says, "he that shall drink of the water that I will give him, shall not thirst for ever." It becomes a spring inside, welling up into everlasting life. And she answers like anyone carrying a heavy jar: Sir, give me this water, so I don't have to keep coming here. She still thinks it's about the walk to the well. Early in its teaching on prayer, the Catechism turns to this scene. It says that Jesus thirsts, and his asking comes from the depth of God's desire for us. Prayer, it says, whether we know it or not, is the meeting of God's thirst with ours. The one who began by asking for a drink is the one who has the water.
screen: `GIVE ME TO DRINK.` · `LIVING WATER: RUNNING WATER.` · `THIS WATER, THIRSTY AGAIN.` · `GOD'S THIRST MEETS OURS.` · then, large: `SHALL NOT THIRST FOR EVER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drink water slowly and pray. Get a glass of water if you can. Settle, and breathe. Lift the glass and feel its weight. Take one slow sip, and notice the cool of it going down. Then another. Think of the thirst underneath this one, if there is one: something you keep going back to the well for, that never quite fills. If you pray, you can ask, as she did, give me this water. If you don't, just drink slowly and pay attention to being thirsty and being given something. The bell holds the time.
Living water. A phrase for running spring water; in John, the gift Jesus offers at Jacob's well that ends thirst for ever. Today's word.
Your line: never thirst. Today, every time you drink water, let it remind you of the one who asked first. Day five hundred.

501.title: White for harvest (John 4:31–38)
501.hook: lift up your eyes: the fields are already white
501.howItsDone: Catholics hear this passage as part of the longer Gospel of the Samaritan woman on the Third Sunday of Lent in Year A, and the Church has often drawn on it in teaching about the mission to share the faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman at Jacob's well, and living water. Your line was never thirst. Did a glass of water remind you of who asked first? Day five hundred one.

While Jesus was talking at the well, the disciples were in town buying lunch. They come back with food and find him talking with a Samaritan woman. They're surprised, but nobody asks. The woman leaves her water jar right there and hurries back into town. Come, and see a man who has told me all things whatsoever I have done. Is not he the Christ? Meanwhile the disciples unpack the food. Rabbi, eat. And he says something that makes them look at each other. I have food to eat that you don't know about. Did someone already bring him lunch?
screen: `THE DISCIPLES BRING LUNCH.` → `SHE LEAVES HER WATER JAR.` → `I HAVE FOOD YOU DON'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: This is John's pattern: Jesus says something deep, and someone takes it at ground level. Born again: back into the womb? Living water: where's your bucket? Food: who brought him a sandwich? Then he explains, in the Douay-Rheims: "My meat is to do the will of him that sent me, that I may perfect his work." Meat is the old word for food. What feeds him is doing his Father's will. And then he points. You have a saying, he tells them: four more months, and then the harvest. Farmers' wisdom. Planting's done, it's a long wait. "Behold, I say to you, lift up your eyes, and see the countries, for they are white already to harvest." Countries here means the fields around them. White, because grain goes pale and gold when it's ripe. But picture what the disciples might actually see when they lift their eyes. Across the fields, coming out of the town, the Samaritans the woman has just told. A crowd walking toward them through the grain. Some readers have even wondered whether the white was the light clothing of that crowd. The text doesn't say. Either way, the harvest isn't four months off. It's walking up the road. Then: one sows and another reaps. You are reaping where others did the hard work. Readers name many sowers: the prophets, John the Baptist, Jesus himself. And here, in a small way, the woman with her jar. The disciples, who were busy with lunch and surprised at the scene, are being told to look up. The harvest was ready, and the first worker in it was the last person they would have picked.
screen: `MY FOOD IS TO DO HIS WILL.` · `FOUR MONTHS AND THEN HARVEST?` · `LIFT UP YOUR EYES.` · `ONE SOWS, ANOTHER REAPS.` · then, large: `WHITE ALREADY TO HARVEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice who is ready to hear. Settle, and breathe. Lift your eyes, literally: look up from the screen, at the room, out the window. Then in your mind, look across the people in your week. Who has been asking questions lately? Who seems open, or lonely, or curious, or ready for a kind word? Maybe someone you'd never have picked. Don't plan a speech. Just notice them. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just keep their face in mind. The bell holds the time.
White for harvest. Fields pale and ripe, ready now, not in four months: Jesus's picture of the Samaritans coming to hear him. Today's word.
Your line: lift up your eyes. Today, look up from your phone three times, and notice one person each time. Day five hundred one.

502.title: Wilt thou be made whole (John 5:1–9)
502.hook: a man ill thirty-eight years is asked if he wants to be healed
502.tomorrow: I am the bread of life
502.howItsDone: Catholics hear the healing at the pool on a weekday of the fourth week of Lent, and pilgrims to Jerusalem visit the excavated pools beside the Church of Saint Anne.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fields white for harvest, and the Samaritans coming up the road. Your line was lift up your eyes. Who did you notice when you looked up? Day five hundred two.

In Jerusalem, near the sheep gate, there's a pool with five porches, covered walkways around the water. The Douay-Rheims calls it Probatica, from the Greek for sheep; most Bibles know it as Bethesda. The porches are full of people: the blind, the lame, the withered, lying on mats, waiting. People said that now and then the water was stirred, and the first one in would be healed. One man has been lying there a very long time. Thirty-eight years, John tells us, under his illness. Today Jesus walks into that crowd, finds him, and asks him a question that sounds almost rude.
screen: `A POOL WITH FIVE PORCHES.` → `A CROWD WAITING FOR THE WATER.` → `THIRTY-EIGHT YEARS.`

segments.voice: Jesus sees him lying there, knows he has been that way a long time, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Wilt thou be made whole?" Do you want to get well? On the surface, it's an absurd question. Of course he does. He has been lying by a healing pool for thirty-eight years. But listen to his answer. He doesn't say yes. "Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pond." Someone always gets there first. It's an explanation, and a lonely one: nobody to help, every time. After thirty-eight years, the story he tells about his life has become: it's never going to be me. Jesus doesn't argue with the story. He doesn't carry him to the water. He says: "Arise, take up thy bed, and walk." And immediately the man is made whole, picks up his mat, and walks. The question matters because healing would change everything. A man who has been ill for thirty-eight years has a whole life built around it: a place to lie, a way of asking, a way of being seen. Being made whole means standing up into a life he doesn't know yet. The Church teaches that God respects our freedom, even in healing; grace is offered, not forced. Two honest notes. Some old manuscripts include a verse about an angel stirring the water; many of the earliest leave it out, and modern Catholic Bibles often put it in a footnote. And this pool is real. Archaeologists near the Church of Saint Anne in Jerusalem found two large pools with a wall between them, which some think explains the five porches.
screen: `WILT THOU BE MADE WHOLE?` · `SIR, I HAVE NO MAN.` · `ARISE, TAKE UP THY BED.` · `A REAL POOL BY SAINT ANNE'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer that question honestly. Settle, and breathe. Think of one place where you've been stuck a long time. A habit, a hurt, a fear, a resentment, a relationship gone flat. Then hear the question, gently: do you want to be made whole? Notice your first answer. Is it a yes, or is it a reason, like his: nobody helps, someone always gets there first? Don't judge it. Just hear it. If you pray, you can give God your honest answer. If you don't, just let yourself know what it is. The bell holds the time.
Wilt thou be made whole. Jesus's question to a man ill for thirty-eight years by the pool of Bethesda, before he told him to rise and walk. Today's word.
screen: `WILT THOU BE MADE WHOLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: wilt thou be made whole. Today, take one small step toward the thing you said you wanted, before the reasons start. Day five hundred two.

503.title: I am the bread of life (John 6:35)
503.hook: the first great I am: whoever comes to me shall not hunger
503.howItsDone: Some Catholic families say a short grace before meals, and the Church reads John 6, the Bread of Life discourse, over several Sundays in late summer of Year B.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pool with five porches, and a question: wilt thou be made whole? What was your honest answer? Day five hundred three.

The day before, on a hillside by the Sea of Galilee, five thousand men sat down on the grass and ate from five barley loaves and two fish, with twelve baskets left over. Then the crowd wanted to take him by force and make him king. He slipped away. Now, the next morning, they've crossed the lake in boats to find him again. And he tells them, plainly: you're looking for me not because you saw signs, but because you ate the bread and were filled. They want more breakfast. He's about to offer them something else.
screen: `FIVE THOUSAND FED ON A HILLSIDE.` → `THEY WANT TO MAKE HIM KING.` → `THEY COME BACK FOR MORE BREAD.`

segments.voice: The crowd pushes back. What sign will you give us? Our fathers ate manna in the desert; Moses gave them bread from heaven. It's a fair challenge. Yesterday's loaves were impressive, but manna fed a whole people for forty years. Jesus corrects them: it wasn't Moses who gave the bread, it's my Father who gives the true bread from heaven. And they say, almost like the woman at the well: Lord, give us always this bread. Then the line, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall not hunger: and he that believeth in me shall never thirst." John's Gospel will come back to this shape again and again: I am, and then a picture. I am the bread of life. The light of the world. The door. The good shepherd. The resurrection and the life. The way, the truth and the life. The true vine. We'll meet most of them in the weeks ahead. Each takes something ordinary and says: this is what I am to you. Bread is about as ordinary as it gets. Not a feast. Not a delicacy. The thing on the table, the thing people need day after day. Not hunger, not thirst: he's not promising they'll never miss a meal. He's speaking of a deeper hunger, the one that comes back no matter how much we eat. Catholics hear this whole chapter as pointing toward the Eucharist, and we'll go further into that tomorrow. Today, stay with the plain image. Bread is daily. The promise is daily too.
screen: `OUR FATHERS ATE MANNA.` · `LORD, GIVE US ALWAYS THIS BREAD.` · `I AM, AND THEN A PICTURE.` · `BREAD: ORDINARY AND DAILY.` · then, large: `I AM THE BREAD OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray before eating. Think of your next meal, or if food is nearby, set it in front of you. Settle, and breathe. Before the first bite, stop. Look at it. Think of the hands that grew it, carried it, cooked it. Some Catholic families say a short grace before meals, such as the old one that begins bless us, O Lord. If you pray, you can say it, or simply give thanks in your own words. If you don't, just pause and let the food be noticed before it's eaten. The bell holds the time.
Manna. What the crowd asked for, remembering the desert, before Jesus answered: I am the bread of life, and whoever comes to me shall not hunger. Today's word.
Your line: bread of life. Today, don't eat your first bite of any meal without a pause. Day five hundred three.

what it means: Jesus offers himself as the daily bread that answers the deepest hunger, and the chapter goes on toward the Eucharist.

504.title: My flesh is meat indeed (John 6:51–58)
504.hook: the Church reads this chapter as the heart of Eucharistic faith (CCC 1336)
504.howItsDone: Catholics receive Communion at Mass believing it is truly the body and blood of Christ, genuflect toward the tabernacle where the consecrated Host is kept, and some spend quiet time in adoration before it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, manna remembered, then the first great I am: I am the bread of life. Your line was bread of life. Did you pause before a first bite? Day five hundred four.

If a friend said, I am your bread, you'd take it as a metaphor. You'd nod. People say things like that. Up to now in John chapter six, the crowd could have done the same. Bread from heaven, coming to him, believing in him: it all sounds like a picture of faith. And then Jesus says something no one can comfortably take as a picture. The crowd hears it and starts arguing out loud. Today is the stretch of the chapter Christians still argue over, and for Catholics it sits at the center of Sunday Mass.
screen: `I AM YOUR BREAD: A METAPHOR?` → `THEN HE GOES FURTHER.` → `THE CROWD ARGUES OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "If any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever; and the bread that I will give, is my flesh, for the life of the world." The listeners argue among themselves: how can this man give us his flesh to eat? It's the natural question. Catholic readers point to what comes next: he doesn't soften it. He says it more strongly: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you. And then: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." Meat is the old word for food. Indeed means truly, really. Some readers notice that John's Greek changes verbs here, to one that can mean chew; others think it's only a change of style. The Catholic Church reads this chapter as the heart of its faith in the Eucharist. The Catechism says the first announcement of the Eucharist divided the disciples, just as the announcement of the cross would later scandalize them. Catholics believe that at Mass the bread and wine become, truly and substantially, the body and blood of Christ, while still looking like bread and wine, and the Council of Trent called that change transubstantiation. Orthodox Christians also hold that Christ is truly present. Protestant churches differ among themselves: some speak of Christ truly or spiritually present, some of a memorial. Today's line, eat, and live, is the Catholic reading in three words: whoever eats this bread will live for ever. It's why Catholics genuflect to the tabernacle, and why the Church asks them to be at Mass every Sunday. They believe they are being fed.
screen: `HOW CAN HE GIVE US HIS FLESH?` · `HE DOESN'T SOFTEN IT.` · `TRULY FOOD, TRULY DRINK.` · `THE HEART OF EUCHARISTIC FAITH.` · then, large: `MY FLESH IS MEAT INDEED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray before the tabernacle. If you're near a Catholic church that's open, you can go in and sit near the tabernacle, where the consecrated Host is kept, with a lamp burning near it. If not, picture one: the candle, the quiet, the box at the front. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to say a lot. Catholics believe Christ is present there, and some simply sit with him the way you'd sit with a friend, saying nothing. If you pray, you can just stay. If you don't, sit with the quiet and the lamp. The bell holds the time.
My flesh is meat indeed. Jesus in John six: his flesh is truly food and his blood truly drink. Catholics read it as the Eucharist. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: eat, and live. Today, notice what actually feeds you. And that's week seventy-two: so loved, bridegroom's friend, living water, white for harvest, made whole, bread of life, and meat indeed. Day five hundred four.
